## Clinical trial data is precious {.flip-bg background-image="assets/content-central/AdobeStock_158958915.jpeg" background-size="cover" background-opacity="0.75"}

::: {.absolute top="120" left="60" width="600" style="background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.7); padding: 8px 16px; border-radius: 12px; text-align: center;" .fragment}
[*How do a patient's pre-treatment biomarker levels affect their response to treatment?*]{style="font-size: 1.25em"}
:::

::: footer
Stock image
:::

::: {.notes}
- The data I work with day to day is from clinical trials for cancer treatments
- pts participating go through a lot 
- this data is extremely precious, get every insight
- one way is answer research questions to understand
- biomarker: lab test measured during trial
- to answer, need to combine many trials
- And here's where things get difficult because the data from these trials is not in the same format, need to harmonize it
:::


## Harmonization is necessary, but tedious & repetitive 

{{< include _manual-workflow-diagram.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
- Harmonization is fancy way to say reformatting from multiple sources to be compatible
- Seems straightforward, but 10 years, way more complicated
- Imagine that I'm working on harmonizing data from 15 different trials, 15 datasets all different
- write custom R code for every data set, transform every column
- and there are many types of data collected
- 😱 
- project explodes, very complicated very fast
- tell you about the workflow, using LLMs and reproducible pipeline code to automate and simplify this process
:::


## LLM-assisted data harmonization pipeline

{{< include _llm-workflow-diagram.qmd >}}

```{=html}
<div class="fragment fade-out" data-fragment-index="8" style="position: absolute; left: 330px; bottom: 30px; font-size: 150px; line-height: 1;">👩🏻‍💻</div>
<div class="fragment fade-in"  data-fragment-index="8" style="position: absolute; left: 330px; bottom: 30px; font-size: 150px; line-height: 1;">🎉</div>
```

::: {.notes}
- 3 big pieces, data model + pipeline one time
- pipeline: runs harmonization logic to produce harmonized output
- data model: set of yaml, specify what output should look like, variable names, definitions, data types, units, etc.; LLMs
- configs: yamls, map format of original dataset to data model, so pipeline code can compare and do appropriate transformations
  - one PER DATASET PER TRIAL; LLMs
- complicated workflow with custom code for every dataset x trial -> simplified workflow with repetitive work done by LLM
- 🎉
- Save months of work, more questions
- I'll go over LLM-drafted, then how pipeline code brings together; specific to my use case but call out broadly useful approaches
:::

## Pilot project insights

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="75%"}
[❶ Use [data dictionaries]{.bms-purple}, not actual data]{style="font-size: 2em; display: inline-block; margin: 1em 0.5em 0em;" .fragment}

[❷ LLMs and humans have different constraints]{style="font-size: 2em; display: inline-block; margin: 1em 0.5em 0em;" .fragment}
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
![Eslam Abousamra, MPH<br>2025 intern](assets/eslam-abousamra.jpeg){.nostretch fig-align="center"  style="display: inline-block; margin: 2em 0.5em;"}
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
- Work so far building model + configs started during pilot project, internship by Eslam, exceptional, CUNY School of Public Health Phd student, highlight some insights
- 1 Data dictionaries: simpler file describing the data, easier for LLM to work on, fewer tokens, less context than sometimes-large files
  - HW talk yesterday saw how useful these files can be with LLMs
  - Looking into using data-dict.yaml spec later
- 2 Design for LLMs, not humans
  - Years of experience, do it all on demographics, simplest, one row per patient, easy to understand like age, height
  - Ran into trouble -- too many columns, had to pivot to another dataset and then come back and develop chunking approach
:::


## Harmonize a dataset with modular code + configs

::: {.notes}
- Now I'll show pipeline code that brings Eslam's work on the data model and configs together
- 1 transform one dataset from one trial
  - Simplified code, inputs, read orig dataset
  - Plain tidyverse for select, rename
  - Customized functions for complex transforms like data types, units of measure
    - baseline_height_cm example
    - These functions can be unit tested and reused without repeatedly re-writing code
- Now one function call for one dataset in one trial
:::

- take process out of one-time LLM back and forth to make it reproducible, encapsulated in Claude Code plugin
- user harmonize trial, get help with ... (result of each step)

:::


## Takeaways

::: {style="width: 80%; margin-left:3em;"}
[Be flexible to rapid change]{.fragment style="font-size: 2em; display: inline-block; margin-top: 0.75em; margin-bottom: 0em;"}
[AWS Bedrock agent → langchain agent → Claude Code plugin]{.fragment style="font-size: 1em; display: inline-block; margin-top: 0.5em; margin-bottom: 0em; margin-left: 3em; color: #79736E;"}

[Design with structured files]{.fragment style="font-size: 2em; display: inline-block; margin-top: 0.75em; margin-bottom: 0em;"}
[.yaml or .json or even .xml]{.fragment style="font-size: 1em; display: inline-block; margin-top: 0.5em; margin-bottom: 0em; margin-left: 3em; color: #79736E;"}

[Look for data wrangling patterns]{.fragment style="font-size: 2em; display: inline-block; margin-top: 0.75em; margin-bottom: 0em;"}
:::

::: {.notes}
- point out approaches you can use, whether working on data harmonization or not
- Flexible, not locked into any one tech allowed quick pivots as company recommendations changed
- Part of the flexibility was using structured files (makes it easier for LLM to reason about your data)
  - Seeing more and more cause so useful for LLMs
  - e.g. specification-driven development, HW data-dict.yaml
- It's still important to break out your repetitive code into functions
  - If you can make it into a function, you make it into a tool call an LLM can use
:::
